title: Records of the Three Kingdoms
subtitle: The Brush of Official History · True Heroic Character · Restoring the Three Kingdoms
description: "Records of the Three Kingdoms" (Sanguozhi), written by Chen Shou of the Western Jin dynasty, comprises 65 chapters covering the history of the three kingdoms of Wei, Shu, and Wu. It is one of the "First Four Histories" of the "Twenty-Four Histories" and is widely regarded as the most rigorously judged historical work. Unlike later "Romance of the Three Kingdoms" with its fictionalized elements, "Records of the Three Kingdoms" restores the true faces of historical figures such as Cao Cao, Liu Bei, and Sun Quan through the historian's brush. This route, based on "Records of the Three Kingdoms," uses nationally protected cultural relics to restore historical truth.

route.title: Journey Through the Records of the Three Kingdoms: Between Official History and Romance
route.intro:
The mighty Yangzi River flows eastward, its waves sweeping away all heroes.
Chen Shou (233–297), a native of Anhan in Baxi (present-day Nanchong, Sichuan), was originally a Shu Han official. After Shu fell, he entered Jin service, eventually rising to the post of Palace Attendant Imperial Secretary. "Records of the Three Kingdoms" takes Wei as the legitimate line but balances coverage across the "Book of Wei," "Book of Shu," and "Book of Wu." Contemporaries praised him as "skilled in narrative, possessing the talent of a fine historian." Eighteen centuries have passed. Most Chinese people's knowledge of the Three Kingdoms comes from "Romance of the Three Kingdoms"—the Peach Garden Oath, Borrowing Arrows with Straw Boats, the Empty City Strategy, Guan Yu Slaying Hua Xiong While His Wine Is Still Warm. Yet the majority of these beloved stories are Luo Guanzhong's artistic inventions. The accounts in "Records of the Three Kingdoms" are far more sober: Guan Yu did not pass through five passes and slay six generals, Zhuge Liang did not borrow the eastern wind, and Zhou Yu was not driven to death by rage. Yet the official history of the Three Kingdoms is equally fascinating, even richer in human depth. Let us follow six nationally protected Three Kingdoms sites and discover what "Records of the Three Kingdoms" truly recorded, restoring the historical truths obscured by fiction.

stops.title: Stop One: Wuhou Shrine in Chengdu: The True Face of Zhuge Liang
stops.content: Zhuge Liang in the romance: feathered fan and silk kerchief, divine strategies, borrowing the eastern wind, seven captures of Meng Huo, six campaigns from Qishan, the empty city strategy, trapping Sima Yi in the Shangfang Valley—a demigod. Zhuge Liang in "Records of the Three Kingdoms": "Since youth, Liang possessed outstanding talent and heroic ambition. He was eight feet tall and strikingly handsome." Chen Shou held him in the highest regard—"He could truly be called a fine administrator, comparable to Guan Zhong and Xiao He." Yet he also objectively noted: "But though he moved the masses year after year, he did not succeed. Perhaps the arts of adaptation and military command were not his forte." In plain language: Zhuge Liang was a first-rate statesman but not the greatest military commander. His six northern campaigns from Qishan wasted Shu-Han's national strength without tangible results—this is an incontrovertible historical fact. The Chengdu Wuhou Shrine is China's only temple where a ruler and his minister are jointly enshrined. After Liu Bei declared himself emperor in 221 AD, he built the Huiling Mausoleum. Originally the Wuhou Shrine and the Zhaolie Temple stood side by side; in the early Ming, the Prince of Shu, Zhu Chun, ordered them combined on the principle that "ruler and minister should not be separate." The existing buildings were reconstructed in the Kangxi reign of the Qing dynasty, covering 150,000 square meters. Passing through Liu Bei's hall into Zhuge Liang's hall, you feel a strange historical atmosphere: the chancellor deified for eighteen centuries was in fact a man—with talents and limitations, with successes and regrets. And it is precisely this truth of being "human" that commands even greater respect.

stops.title: Stop Two: Zhuge Liang's Tomb in Mian County: The General Star Falls at Mount Dingjun
stops.content: Zhuge Liang's death in the romance: at Wuzhangyuan, he tried to extend his life by lighting the Seven Stars Lamp; Wei Yan accidentally kicked out the lamp; he bequeathed his military manual to Jiang Wei and sent a wooden statue to frighten Sima Yi. Zhuge Liang's death in "Records of the Three Kingdoms": In the twelfth year of the Jianxing reign (234 AD), Zhuge Liang led his army through Xie Gorge and camped at Wuzhangyuan, facing Sima Yi. "They confronted each other for over a hundred days. In the eighth month of that year, Liang fell ill and died in the army, at the age of fifty-four." No star-extending, no seven-star lamp—just exhaustion from overwork. After Zhuge Liang's death, "when the army withdrew, Sima Yi inspected his camp, the disposition of his positions, and said: 'A genius under heaven!'" This remark by Sima Yi carries more weight than any fictional story in the romance. The Wuhou Tomb is at the foot of Mount Dingjun in Mian County, Shaanxi. In his dying testament, Zhuge Liang instructed: "Bury me on Mount Dingjun in Hanzhong. Build the tomb following the mountain's contours; let the grave be just large enough for a coffin. Bury me in my everyday clothes, with no funerary objects." No lavish burial, no grand construction—just burial in his daily clothes, a grave big enough for a coffin. What extraordinary simplicity of character! The cemetery is shaded by dozens of ancient cypresses, said to have been planted in his time. Standing on Mount Dingjun, gazing at the twilight over the Hanzhong Plain, you understand—true greatness needs no mythic embellishment.

stops.title: Stop Three: The Ancient City of Han-Wei Luoyang: The True Face of Cao Cao
stops.content: Cao Cao in the romance: white-faced villain, "I would rather betray the world than have the world betray me," murdering the entire Lü Boshe family, killing in his sleep, seventy-two decoy tombs—a thoroughly sinister and ruthless warlord. Cao Cao in "Records of the Three Kingdoms": Chen Shou evaluates him: "The Grand Progenitor possessed strategic brilliance, brandishing his whip over the realm. He employed the techniques of Shen Buhai and Shang Yang and the extraordinary stratagems of Han Xin and Bai Qi. He assigned official posts according to ability, made emotional concessions while calculating rationally, and bore no grudges. In the end, he was able to take control of the imperial machinery and achieve a great enterprise—this was because he was supreme in strategic planning. He may truly be called a man of extraordinary talents, a surpassing hero of the age." Cao Cao was a statesman, a military commander, and a poet—"Facing wine, let us sing; how few are the days of a man's life!" came from his brush, as did "Bones lie exposed in the wild; for a thousand miles, no cock crows." He implemented agricultural colonies, promoted merit, and curbed the powerful. And he never claimed the imperial title in his lifetime—"If Heaven's mandate lies with me, let me be King Wen of the Zhou." The Ancient City of Han-Wei Luoyang (Including Biyong Stele) served as capitals for four dynasties: Eastern Han, Cao Wei, Western Jin, and Northern Wei. Here Cao Cao held the emperor hostage to command the feudal lords; here Cao Pi accepted the abdication of Emperor Xian of Han and established the Wei state. The city site covers 100 square kilometers, with three layers: palace city, inner city, and outer city. The Biyong Stele is a precious Han-Jin stone inscription. Standing amid the Luoyang ruins, recalling Chen Shou's words—"extraordinary man, surpassing hero of the age"—perhaps we should reconsider that historical giant, so often simplified by the opera masks.

stops.title: Stop Four: Nanjing: Sun Quan's Jiangdong Hegemony
stops.content: Sun Quan in the romance: indecisive, wavering between Cao Cao and Liu Bei, impressive at the Battle of Red Cliffs but lackluster thereafter. Sun Quan in "Records of the Three Kingdoms": Chen Shou evaluates, "Sun Quan humbled himself and endured humiliation, employed talent and valued strategy. He had the brilliance of Gou Jian of Yue and was a hero among men. Thus he was able to make himself master of the region south of the Yangzi, achieving a tripartite balance of power." Cao Cao once exclaimed: "A son should be like Sun Zhongmou!" Sun Quan inherited his father's and elder brother's enterprise at eighteen—he was only twenty-six at the Battle of Red Cliffs. Allied with Liu Bei, he defeated Cao Cao's claimed 800,000 troops with just 50,000. He expanded territory and sent Wei Wen to Yizhou (present-day Taiwan), the first written record of official contact between the mainland and Taiwan in Chinese history. Nanjing became the Wu capital under Sun Quan. In 211 AD, Sun Quan moved his administrative seat from Jingkou (Zhenjiang) to Moling, renaming it Jianye. The following year, he built the precursor of the Nanjing City Wall—the Stone City—guarding the natural barrier of the Yangzi River. Though the existing wall dates mainly from the Ming dynasty, Sun Quan's act began Nanjing's glorious history as capital of six dynasties. Entering Nanjing, you can visit the Stone City ruins at the foot of Qingliang Mountain. Sun Quan built the city by taking advantage of the mountain: "the mountain forms the city walls, the river forms the moat"—the Yangzi River once flowed past the city walls. To this day, a section known as "Ghost Face Wall" bears exposed ochre-red rock, like a menacing ghost face, a mark of time's erosion. Eighteen centuries ago, the Wu navy set out from here, their "ten thousand vessels floating on the river"—a fleet so vast that Cao Wei looked on in awe. The Battle of Red Cliffs established the tripartite division, and Sun Quan ruled in Jiangdong for decades, transforming the southern wasteland into a fertile land of fish and rice. Chen Shou's "Book of Wu" records Sun Quan's art of employing talent: the successive emergence of outstanding figures like Zhou Yu, Lu Su, Lü Meng, and Lu Xun—"a multitude of talented men"—this was the root of his standing in Jiangdong. The "Book of Wu" in "Records of the Three Kingdoms" portrays a kingdom that stood equally with Wei and Shu, whose silk, shipbuilding, and maritime trade reached the highest levels of the world at that time.

stops.title: Stop Five: The Cao Family Tombs in Bozhou: The Family Foundations of a Warlord
stops.content: The Cao family in the romance: apart from Cao Cao himself, Cao Pi is scheming, Cao Zhi is brilliant, Cao Zhang is brave—all wearing stylized masks. The Cao family in "Records of the Three Kingdoms": Cao Pi "was widely learned with a strong memory, and was skilled in many talents." His "Discourse on Literature" in the "Classics" is a foundational work of Chinese literary criticism—"Literature is the great enterprise of governing the state, an immortal achievement." The story of Cao Zhi composing a poem in seven steps does not appear in "Records of the Three Kingdoms," but Chen Shou says he "was rich and brilliant in literary talent, enough to transmit his name to posterity." Cao Zhang was indeed brave: "from youth, he was skilled in archery and horsemanship, of extraordinary physical strength, able to fight wild beasts bare-handed." Cao Cao placed great emphasis on his sons' education; the three Caos—father and sons—were known collectively as the "Three Caos," building the pinnacle of Jian'an literature. The Cao Family Tombs in Bozhou, Anhui, are the burial ground of Cao Cao's clan, including the tombs of Cao Teng and Cao Song, yielding precious artifacts such as a silver-thread jade burial suit. Cao Teng was Cao Cao's grandfather, a powerful eunuch of the late Eastern Han; Cao Song was Cao Cao's father, who rose to Grand Commandant. These tombs reveal the material foundation of a prominent family—Cao Cao's extraordinary talents did not come from nowhere; he inherited a family that had accumulated political capital over several generations. More intriguing is Cao Cao's ancestry. According to "Records of the Three Kingdoms—Annals of Emperor Wu," Cao Song was Cao Teng's adopted son—"none could determine his origins"—even the background of Cao Song himself was unclear. This differs from the romance's claim that "Cao Cao's original surname was Xiahou"; the official history does not settle this question. The rise of the Cao family reflects the political ecology of the late Eastern Han, where eunuchs and imperial in-laws alternated in power: how a eunuch family accumulated enough capital to compete for the realm is itself a textbook of power politics. The artifacts from the Cao tombs displayed in the Bozhou Museum—silver-thread jade suits, copper-thread jade suits, jade pigs, pottery towers—each tells of real life during that era of great upheaval. Bozhou also has the legendary Cao Cao Underground Military Tunnel—a rare surviving ancient military tunnel site. The fascinating thing about history is that the details provided by official records are often more intriguing than fiction.

stops.title: Stop Six: The Cao-Wei New City at Hefei: The Real Battlefield of Xiaoyao Ford
stops.content: The Battle of Hefei in the romance: Zhang Liao's might shakes Xiaoyao Ford, so feared that even Wu children dared not cry at night. Eight hundred men defeat 100,000—a heavily romanticized legend. The Battle of Hefei in "Records of the Three Kingdoms": In the twentieth year of the Jian'an reign (215 AD), Sun Quan led 100,000 troops to besiege Hefei. The defending general Zhang Liao, "armed with armor and halberd, led the charge into the fray, killing scores of men and two enemy generals," charging straight to Sun Quan's command post. "Sun Quan, greatly alarmed, did not know what to do." Yet the romance's claim of "eight hundred breaking one hundred thousand" is indeed an exaggeration—"Records of the Three Kingdoms" clearly states Zhang Liao led "eight hundred men," but does not specify Sun Quan's casualties. The key point: Zhang Liao's surprise attack did intimidate Sun Quan, and combined with Hefei's strong walls and an epidemic, Sun Quan eventually withdrew. The Cao-Wei New City Site at Hefei in Luyang District, Hefei, is a military fortress built by the famous Wei general Man Chong. During the Three Kingdoms period, Hefei was the focus of contention between Wei and Wu—whoever controlled Hefei held the initiative on the Jianghuai battlefield. The site preserves rammed-earth city walls, a city gate, a barbican, and other features with clear outlines. Most valuably, the Cao-Wei New City at Hefei is one of the best-preserved Three Kingdoms military fortress sites. When Man Chong built it, he chose high ground west of the Fei River, enabling both water transport and a commanding view of the battlefield. The walls were built in layered rammed-earth sections, each layer about ten centimeters thick, as hard as stone. Within the city, large palace foundations, training grounds, and reservoirs have been discovered. Archaeologists have unearthed large quantities of iron weapons, chariot and horse fittings, and everyday utensils—those rusted iron arrowheads once pierced the clouds above the battlefield. Chen Shou, in the "Biography of Man Chong" in "Records of the Three Kingdoms," records the circumstances of the new city's construction—a rare military project that can be fully reconstructed through archaeological site. Standing on the site, you can feel that while Zhang Liao's famous victory was at the old Hefei city, this new city witnessed decades of back-and-forth struggle between Wei and Wu—history is not a single stroke of legend, but a long process full of contingencies.
